chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from one of his men, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about the testimony when it is established upon the truth: is it permissible for the judge to rule based on the testimony if he does not know them without questioning? He said: There are five things upon which people must rely on the apparent ruling: guardianships, marriages, inheritances, slaughtering, and testimonies. So when its apparent is reliable, his testimony is accepted, and its inner reality is not questioned.

key_terms.الْبَاطِن: The inner reality (truth behind the appearance)

ai.seo_question: What are the five categories in Shia law where judges rely on apparent evidence without questioning inner truth?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi articulates the jurisprudential principle of 'Zuhur al-Hukm' (the apparent ruling), establishing that in five key social domains—guardianship, marriage, inheritance, slaughtering, and testimonies—the judge relies on the outward reliability (zahir) of the individual without delving into their inner truth (batin). This doctrine, central to Shia fiqh, ensures legal stability and practicality by accepting the public status of individuals as valid unless proven otherwise, reflecting the Shi'a emphasis on the continuity of social order through apparent evidence.
